content: Scientists at Columbia University have discovered that electron waves can become trapped inside a metal, even when pathways remain available for them to escape. The finding, published in Science , provides the first experimental evidence of a long-predicted quantum phenomenon in a metallic material. The trapped waves were found near atomic defects in a metal called Pd5AlI2. Unlike electrons that move freely through conducting materials, these waves remain confined because of quantum interference. “Bound electrons shouldn’t occur in a metal, but they do in Pd5AlI2. What we have observed is the first clear evidence of quantum interference trapping a state in a metal,” said Columbia theoretical physicist Raquel Queiroz. Quantum mechanics describes electrons as waves that can travel along multiple possible paths. When these waves overlap, they can reinforce or cancel one another. Under certain conditions, destructive interference can prevent an electron wave from spreading, even when other electron states can move through the same material. This phenomenon is called a bound state in the continuum (BIC). “Quantum mechanics predicts that an electron wave can, theoretically, remain trapped even when there are infinitely many paths for it to escape. This effect is known from light waves, but it has never been seen before for electrons,” said Queiroz. The discovery began in Columbia chemist Xavier Roy’s laboratory, where researchers developed Pd5AlI2, a metal that can be separated into thin, two-dimensional layers while retaining its metallic properties. Measurements showed that its electrons moved more slowly than expected. Working with Queiroz and experimental physicists Cory Dean and Aravind Devarakonda (a former Columbia postdoc who is now an assistant professor of applied physics at Columbia), the team traced this behavior to electron hopping frustration. The metal’s atomic structure creates competing paths for electrons to move between atoms, allowing destructive interference to suppress their movement. The findings were published in Nature Physics . Researchers working with Columbia physicist Abhay Pasupathy later detected unexpected patterns while examining Pd5AlI2 using atomic-scale scanning and spectroscopy techniques. Further analysis revealed electron waves trapped near defects in the crystal lattice. Queiroz developed theoretical models explaining how quantum interference produced these localized states. Bound states in the continuum have previously been demonstrated with light, where they have helped advance lasers, optical sensing, and nonlinear optics. The Columbia findings establish that a similar effect can occur with electrons in metals. “Trapping a wave is an idea as old as quantum mechanics itself, but it took almost a century to figure out how to do it with light. We have now realized it with electrons in a material,” said Roy. “And if you trap a particle, you can manipulate it.” Electronic bound states could eventually contribute to highly sensitive quantum sensors, quantum information processing, and quantum chemistry. However, controlling their formation remains a challenge. In Pd5AlI2, the electron traps form around defects that arise randomly during crystal growth. Roy and Pasupathy are now investigating ways to deliberately position these defects and control the resulting interference patterns. The discovery also offers a way to identify other metals with frustrated crystal structures that could support trapped electron waves. Reference: “Electronic bound states in the continuum in a two-dimensional metal” by Morgan Thinel, Xiong Huang, Daniel G. Chica, Simon Turkel, Sebastian E. Rossi, Christie S. Koay, Hong Li, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Bipasa Samanta, Madisen Holbrook, Aravind Devarakonda, Luca M. Nashabeh, Alexandru B. Georgescu, Xavier Roy, Xiaoyang Zhu, Abhay N. Pasupathy and Raquel Queiroz, 22 October 2026, Science . title: How to catch the hunter’s moon this weekend — and maybe Saturn, too
content: October’s full moon will grace the sky this weekend — and those with a keen eye may also catch a glimpse of Saturn. Just a month after the fall equinox , the full moon will rise particularly early, becoming visible at sunset and reaching peak illumination at 12:12 a.m. ET on Monday, October 26, according to EarthSky . As night falls on Sunday, Saturn also will appear gold and sit just a few degrees south of the moon. The orb may look more orange as it hangs lower on the horizon. This position causes the moonlight to pass through a denser layer of air, shortening blue and violet wavelengths and making the orange and red ones stand out — similar to a sunset. Named the hunter’s moon, Native Americans traditionally took advantage of the bright moonlight to hunt for active wildlife and prepare food for the winter. October’s full moon follows September’s harvest moon , which marked when farmers would typically harvest their crops. “These names were assigned to the moon because the moon has a meaning,” said Noah Petro, chief of NASA’s Planetary Geology, Geophysics and Geochemistry Lab at Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland. “I’d encourage folks, while they’re looking at the moon, to ask, ‘What does this time of year mean to me?’ Everyone should have a personal connection.” Other monikers for the hunter’s moon are similarly rooted in seasonal traditions. Indigenous tribes adopted names including the drying rice moon, the falling leaves moon and the migrating moon. Some groups also referred to it as the blood moon, a nod to its orange-red hue. The full moon will appear its usual silvery color over the next several months, but viewers who look closely will notice the moon’s face shifting as it rotates, said Petro, who is also a project scientist for the Artemis III mission . The moon owes its varying gradation to differences in surface composition and age — something Petro’s team plans to explore in the Artemis mission slated for June 2027. “When you see color differences on the moon, that’s telling you that something has already happened there — either the rocks are made of something different, or it’s a younger or older surface,” Petro said. “It tells you about the geological history.” For optimal sky-gazing, Petro suggested finding a place free of obstruction from trees or buildings, such as a large field. He added that cold winter nights can make it easier to see the moon, because heat generates turbulence in the atmosphere and makes the sky hazy. “The beauty of the moon is that you don’t need to have the most impressive telescope,” Petro said. “You need two things: clear eyes and clear skies. And with that, you can fall in love with the moon.” If the sky isn’t clear Sunday night, the moon will appear full on Saturday and Monday as well. The hunter’s moon comes at the end of a several-day period of the orb approaching and passing Saturn. The ringed planet may be difficult to spot because of the moon’s luminescence. Sky-gazing opportunities aren’t over after this weekend’s dual visual treat. From Monday to Wednesday, the moon will approach, eclipse and pass the Pleiades star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters. Appearing to the unaided eye as a fuzzy collection of six to seven stars, the Pleiades is among the most well-known celestial clusters across the world. The hunter’s moon marks 11 out of 13 full moons in 2026. The final two are both supermoons, meaning the satellite will appear brighter and larger because it is closest to Earth in its orbit.
